markers.title: Sort by what happens if nobody acts
markers.finding: The list was long, flat and uniform, so managers dismissed warnings without investigating them. There was no documentation of a dismissal and no oversight of the decision.
markers.decision: Two panels before any row: what is clear, and what needs a decision broken down by consequence. Stops the roster or costs money. Breaches a rule with no automatic cost. Worth knowing.
markers.rejected: Severity by rule category, which is how the original list was grouped and which tells a manager nothing about what to do first.

markers.title: A warning belongs to a person
markers.finding: Warnings belonged to the screen. Nobody owned one, so nobody was accountable for clearing it, and area coaches compiled their own spot checks by hand.
markers.decision: Every row carries an owner and a date to fix it by. Five of the six are the rostering manager's and two of them are on the same day, which is a morning's work rather than a backlog.
markers.rejected: A send-a-message action as the only response, which chases the person rather than changing the roster.

markers.title: Every warning carries its price
markers.finding: Ignoring a warning had no visible consequence until the pay run, when make-up pay, overtime and compliance pay appeared without explanation.
markers.decision: The subtitle on each row is what it costs or what it breaches. A manager triaging six items can see which two are money.
markers.rejected: A severity word alone, which is a judgement the product is asking the manager to trust rather than a figure they can weigh.

markers.title: Dismissal is a record with a reason
markers.finding: Dismissals happened under time pressure with nothing recorded, which was raised as a backlog item for compliance pay dismissal mitigation.
markers.decision: Dismissing asks which of three situations applies and writes a note that stays on the shift and reaches the area coach's weekly report. Three dismissals of one rule in a month raise it automatically.
markers.rejected: A confirm dialog, which records that somebody clicked and nothing about why.
